finding.claim: PUT /doc/<doc_id> (update_doc) computes can_edit(g.user, doc) but discards the result and never aborts, so any authenticated user can overwrite the body of any document they do not own or edit.
finding.source: URL segment doc_id and JSON body field of the PUT request; caller needs only to be authenticated so that g.user is set (set by middleware not in this file).
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20 (protected document body write).

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> accepts any doc_id from the URL.
doc = DOCS[doc_id] loads the target document.
can_edit(g.user, doc) evaluated but its boolean result is discarded; no abort(403).
can_edit has no side effects; it only returns a boolean (owner or in editors).
Attacker-supplied request.json['body'] is written into the document.
Handler returns ok=True, confirming the unauthorized write.

finding.guards_checked: can_edit logic (docs.py:7-8) is correct but unenforced at line 19; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) correctly aborts 403 but is not called on this route; no authentication decorator or ownership check on this route in this file; sibling update_title (docs.py:27) correctly calls require_edit, so it is not affected. Unverified: where g.user is set, and whether cookie-based auth requires CSRF protection on this JSON PUT.

verdict.guard_found: none effective on the update_doc route. can_edit (docs.py:7-8) returns a bool, but its call at docs.py:19 is a bare statement whose result is discarded, so no 403 is raised. require_edit (docs.py:11-13) would abort, but it is not called on this route (it is only used by update_title at docs.py:27). No before_request hook or ownership check appears in this file. g.user is set outside this file, but that only requires authentication, not ownership.
verdict.reason: The PUT handler at docs.py:19 evaluates can_edit(g.user, doc) and discards the boolean, so the body write at docs.py:20 runs for any authenticated user, while the sibling update_title at docs.py:27 correctly uses require_edit. The attacker only needs a valid session, which is a low-privilege role that does not already hold the power, so this is a real authorization bypass.
